title: Goroutines and channels
summary: Cheap concurrency, blocking as the default, and the ways it stops.

concepts.title: Goroutines
concepts.brief:
`go f()` runs `f` concurrently and returns immediately. The goroutine starts with a couple of kilobytes of stack that grows as needed, so hundreds of thousands of them is normal where hundreds of OS threads would not be.

Two rules that catch everyone:

- **You cannot get a return value.** `go f()` discards whatever `f` returns, including its error. Results come back over a channel or via a shared variable under a lock.
- **When `main` returns, the program exits**, and every other goroutine is killed mid-step with no `defer` run and no warning.

examples.label: Waiting for a group of them
examples.note: `Add` must happen before the `go`, not inside the goroutine — otherwise `Wait` can run before the counter was ever raised and return immediately.

examples.label: main does not wait
examples.note: The goroutine is scheduled but the process exits before it runs. This is also why a background worker with no `wg.Wait()` silently does nothing in a short-lived job.

items.prompt: `go doWork()` where `doWork` returns `error`. How do you get the error?
choices: Not from the go statement — send it on a channel or collect it under a lock
Assign it: `err := go doWork()`
Read it from the goroutine's exit status after wg.Wait()
Recover it in the parent, since a returned error surfaces as a panic
items.explain: `go` is a statement, not an expression — there is nowhere for a value to go. This is the single biggest source of silently swallowed errors in Go services: work is fired off with `go`, it fails, and nothing ever learns. `errgroup.Group` exists mostly to solve this.

items.prompt: `func main() { go fmt.Println("hello") }` — what does it print?
choices: Usually nothing — main returns and the process exits before it runs
hello, reliably
hello, but only on a multi-core machine
Nothing, and it deadlocks on exit
items.explain: The process exits when `main` returns, taking every goroutine with it — no `defer` runs, no cleanup, nothing flushed. It is a race you usually lose, which is worse than always losing it, because it will occasionally work on your laptop.

items.prompt: Put the correct use of a WaitGroup for one worker in order.
steps: Inside it, defer wg.Done() so it runs even on a panic
wg.Wait() blocks in the caller until the counter reaches zero
items.explain: `Add` before `go` is the part that matters. Put `wg.Add(1)` inside the goroutine and `Wait` may run first, see zero, and return while nothing has started. And `Done` belongs in a `defer` — a worker that panics and is recovered higher up would otherwise leave `Wait` blocked forever.

items.prompt: Roughly what does an idle goroutine cost, and what does that imply?
choices: A couple of KB of stack that grows on demand — tens of thousands is routine
The same as an OS thread, around 1 MB — keep a pool
A full OS thread each, which is why a worker pool is mandatory
One OS thread each, capped by GOMAXPROCS
items.explain: A small growable stack, multiplexed onto a few OS threads by the runtime. That is why `net/http` can start one per connection without a pool. The flip side is that leaking them is easy and cheap enough to go unnoticed until there are 20,000.

concepts.title: Channels
concepts.brief:
A typed pipe between goroutines, where **blocking is the point**.

- **Unbuffered** (`make(chan T)`) — a rendezvous. The send completes only when a receiver takes the value; both sides wait for the other.
- A **buffered channel** (`make(chan T, n)`) — the send completes while there is room, and blocks when the buffer is full.

Closing is a broadcast, not a cleanup. Receives from a closed channel return the **zero value immediately**, forever; `v, ok := <-ch` sets `ok` false, and `for v := range ch` ends.

Only the sender should close, because sending on a closed channel panics and there is no way to ask whether a channel is closed.

examples.label: The panics, and the one that hangs
examples.code:
ch := make(chan int)
close(ch)

<-ch              // fine: returns 0 immediately, forever
v, ok := <-ch     // v == 0, ok == false

ch <- 1           // panic: send on closed channel
close(ch)         // panic: close of closed channel

var nilCh chan int
nilCh <- 1        // blocks forever - no panic, just gone
<-nilCh           // also blocks forever
close(nilCh)      // panic: close of nil channel
examples.note: The nil channel is the quiet one: it is not an error, it simply never proceeds. A nil channel in a `select` disables that case, which is occasionally useful on purpose.

examples.label: Ranging until closed
examples.note: Without the `close`, this `range` blocks forever after the fifth job — and if it is the only goroutine left, the runtime reports a deadlock.

items.prompt: `ch := make(chan int)` and one goroutine does `ch <- 1`. No one is receiving yet. What happens?
choices: The send blocks until some goroutine receives
The value is queued and the send returns immediately
It panics — an unbuffered channel cannot hold a value
The value is dropped and the send returns
items.explain: An unbuffered channel has nowhere to put the value, so the send waits for a receiver to meet it. That is the synchronization: after the send completes, you know a receiver has it. It is also how a result channel leaks a goroutine when the receiver gives up first.

items.prompt: Match each operation on a *closed* channel to what it does.
pairs: Returns the zero value immediately, every time
ok is false — how you detect the close
items.explain: Receiving is safe and sending is fatal, which is the whole reason the convention is that only the sender closes. With multiple senders you need something else — a `sync.Once`, or a separate done channel that they all watch.

items.prompt: `for j := range jobs` and the producer finishes without calling `close(jobs)`.
choices: The loop blocks forever waiting for a value that never comes
The loop ends when the buffer empties
The loop ends when the producer goroutine returns
It panics with 'range over unclosed channel'
items.explain: `range` over a channel ends only on close — it has no other way to know the stream is finished. If that consumer is the last runnable goroutine you get `fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!`; if anything else is still running, you just hang quietly, which is worse.

items.prompt: `var ch chan int` — never made. You send on it.
choices: It blocks forever — no panic, no error
It panics with 'send on nil channel'
It succeeds; nil channels discard values
It does not compile
items.explain: Sends and receives on a nil channel block forever. Unlike the nil map there is no panic to tell you — the goroutine parks and never returns, showing up in a profile as `chan send (nil chan)`. Closing one is the exception: `close(nil)` panics with `close of nil channel`. The usual cause of all three is a struct field nobody initialized.

items.prompt: Write the expression making a channel of `string` that can hold one value without a receiver.
items.explain: `make(chan string, 1)`. This exact shape is the fix for the leaked result goroutine: one buffered slot means the send always completes, so the sender always exits even when the receiver has already timed out and gone.

concepts.title: Channels or a mutex
concepts.brief:
The proverb is *"don't communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating"* — but it is advice, not a law, and the standard library is full of mutexes.

- **A channel** suits handing *ownership* of a value from one goroutine to another: pipelines, work queues, results, signals.
- **A mutex** suits protecting *state that stays put*: a cache, a counter, a map of connections.

Using a channel where a mutex belongs produces a goroutine whose only job is to own a variable, and a lot of ceremony to read it. The usual mistake is reaching for the clever one.

examples.label: A mutex is the right tool here
examples.note: Pointer receiver, `defer Unlock` so an early return or a panic still releases, and the mutex sits immediately above the thing it guards.

examples.label: RWMutex, when reads dominate
examples.code:
var mu sync.RWMutex

mu.RLock()          // many readers at once
v := cache[key]
mu.RUnlock()

mu.Lock()           // exclusive
cache[key] = v
mu.Unlock()
examples.note: Only worth it when reads heavily outnumber writes — RWMutex has more overhead per operation than a plain Mutex.

items.prompt: You have an in-memory cache read and written by many handlers. Channel or mutex?
choices: A mutex — the state stays in one place and is protected, not handed over
A channel, so access is serialized through one owner goroutine
Neither; maps are safe for concurrent reads and writes
A channel per key, to avoid a global lock
items.explain: A mutex. Channels are for transferring ownership; a cache is shared state that nobody owns exclusively. The channel version needs a dedicated goroutine, a request channel and a reply channel per lookup — far more machinery, and slower.

items.prompt: Why is `defer c.mu.Unlock()` immediately after `Lock()` the standard shape?
choices: It releases the lock on every exit path, including a panic
It makes the lock reentrant
It is faster than calling Unlock directly
It prevents the mutex from being copied
items.explain: Every `return`, and any panic recovered higher up, still unlocks. A manual `Unlock` before one return and not another leaves the mutex held forever, and every other goroutine piles up behind it — a hang with no error anywhere. Go's mutexes are not reentrant, so re-locking in the same goroutine deadlocks it against itself.

items.prompt: Match each job to the tool that fits it.
pairs: A work queue feeding N workers
A shared map of open connections
Waiting for N workers to finish
items.explain: Closing a channel as a broadcast is the one worth remembering: every receiver unblocks at once, which is how `ctx.Done()` works underneath. You cannot do that with a mutex, and you do not need a channel per listener.

items.prompt: Two goroutines increment the same `int` with no lock. What finds it?
choices: `go test -race` — the race detector flags concurrent unsynchronized access
`go vet`, at compile time
The runtime, with a fatal error like it does for maps
Nothing; an int increment is atomic on 64-bit machines
items.explain: `-race` instruments memory access and reports the two stacks involved, which is usually enough to fix it immediately. The runtime has a built-in check for *maps* but not for plain variables, so an unprotected `n++` silently loses updates. `n++` is read-modify-write — never atomic, on any architecture.

concepts.title: Deadlocks and leaks
concepts.brief:
Two different failures that look similar from outside:

- **Deadlock** — every goroutine is blocked. The runtime notices and kills the program with `fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!`.
- **Leak** — *some* goroutines are blocked forever while others keep working. The runtime says nothing, because the program is still making progress.

The leak is the dangerous one. A blocked goroutine is never collected and holds everything it references, so the symptom is memory climbing with no obvious allocation — and it usually correlates with someone else being slow, not with your own traffic.

examples.label: The runtime catches only the total case
examples.code:
fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!

goroutine 1 [chan receive]:
main.main()
        /app/main.go:12 +0x5a
examples.note: Only when *every* goroutine is blocked. One live background goroutine — a ticker, an HTTP server — and the detector stays quiet forever.

examples.label: Counting them is the cheap diagnostic
examples.note: Needs `import _ "net/http/pprof"`. Exporting `runtime.NumGoroutine()` as a metric gives you the same signal on a dashboard.

items.prompt: Why does a leaked goroutine in an HTTP server never trigger the deadlock detector?
choices: It fires only when every goroutine is blocked; the server is still accepting
It is disabled in production builds
It only covers channels, not mutexes
It only runs during `go test`
items.explain: The detector asks "is anything runnable?" and the answer in a server is always yes. So the one situation where leaks matter most is exactly the one the runtime cannot warn you about. You need the goroutine profile, or a count on a dashboard.

items.prompt: A goroutine is blocked forever on a channel nothing else references. Does the garbage collector clean it up?
choices: No — a blocked goroutine is a root; it and everything it holds stay alive
Yes, once the channel becomes unreachable the goroutine is collected
Yes, after the GC's two-minute idle sweep
Only if it was started with a context
items.explain: The runtime cannot prove it will never run again, so it stays, along with its stack and every variable it captured. This is why goroutine leaks show up as a memory leak: each one pins a request's worth of data that would otherwise have been freed.

items.prompt: A goroutine profile groups stacks by their parked state. Match each state to the counterpart that went missing.
pairs: No receiver — and there never will be one
No sender, or a channel nobody closed
Every case is on a channel that is not ready
A mutex or WaitGroup someone else never released
items.explain: The state names the missing half, which is usually the whole diagnosis. `chan send` in bulk means receivers gave up; `semacquire` in bulk means a lock is held by something stuck. Pair it with the line number the profile groups on and you are looking at the abandoning caller within a minute.

items.prompt: Which of these reliably prevent a result goroutine from leaking when the receiver may give up?
choices: Buffer the channel to the number of values that will be sent
Select on ctx.Done() in the sender so it can abandon the send
Guarantee the receiver always receives, however late
Call runtime.Gosched() before the send
items.explain: Those three are the only shapes that work, and they are the whole list: make the send not block, make the sender able to give up, or make the receiver reliable. `Gosched` just yields the processor — it changes scheduling, never whether a send can complete.
